displayQuote: Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration

meta.title: Who really said "Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, genuinely Thomas Edison. He affirmed the exact wording in a 1927 letter and a 1932 Harper's interview, though it evolved from an earlier 2%/98% version.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Genius is one percent inspiration and ninety-nine percent perspiration'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Thomas Edison — a rare famous quote that holds up. He affirmed the exact wording himself, though the 1%/99% form evolved from an earlier 2%/98% line.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: This is one of the rare famous quotes that holds up. Edison repeated the maxim across interviews for decades, affirmed the exact wording in a 1927 letter (“it is quite true I once made the statement… and I am still of the same opinion”), and was quoted saying it verbatim in M. A. Rosanoff’s September 1932 Harper’s Monthly profile. The one nuance: the polished “1 % / 99 %” form evolved from an earlier “2 % genius, 98 % hard work” version he gave in 1898.

source.heading: The documented source
source.excerpt: None of my inventions came by accident. I see a worthwhile need to be met and I make trial after trial until it comes. What it boils down to is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent perspiration.
trail: The line is traced by Quote Investigator, which credits Edison with formulating the fractional maxim while noting he first gave it (in April 1898) as “two per cent… genius and ninety-eight per cent… hard work.”
The modern 1 %/99 % wording appeared in print attributed to Edison by 1901, and Edison himself affirmed it in a 1927 letter quoted in Wikiquote’s sourced section.
It was cemented in popular memory by M. A. Rosanoff’s September 1932 Harper’s Monthly profile, in which Edison is quoted saying the line verbatim.
source.excerptNote: As quoted by M. A. Rosanoff, who worked in Edison’s laboratory, in Harper’s Monthly Magazine, September 1932. Edison had used variants of the line for decades before this.
source.rightsNote: The saying was first published, attributed to Edison, in 1901 and again in his authorized biography and letters — all well before 1931 — so the wording is in the public domain in the United States. (Rosanoff’s 1932 Harper’s article is a later re-quotation, not the first appearance of the line.)

author.name: Thomas Edison
author.heading: About Thomas Edison
author.bio: Thomas Alva Edison was a prolific American inventor and entrepreneur who developed the phonograph, the long-lasting incandescent light bulb, and the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey. Holding over a thousand US patents, he was famous for his relentless trial-and-error method — a working philosophy that the “inspiration and perspiration” maxim distills. He returned to the line again and again across a long public life, and it became inseparable from his reputation for dogged effort.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Edison is genuine — but the exact wording and its precision are frequently overstated. Two honest wrinkles are worth flagging.

items.why: Edison did not settle on “1 % / 99 %” from the start. His earliest documented version (Ladies’ Home Journal, April 1898) was “Two per cent… genius and ninety-eight per cent… hard work.” The famous 1 %/99 % form is a later refinement, in print by 1901.

The sentiment predates Edison. Lecturer Kate Sanborn framed genius as “perspiration more than inspiration” in the early 1890s, and Thomas Carlyle’s “genius is an infinite capacity for taking pains” circulated earlier still. Edison sharpened the thought into its memorable percentage form.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: genuinely Edison — he coined the fractional maxim and affirmed the exact wording himself — but the polished “1 % / 99 %” version evolved from his earlier “2 % / 98 %” phrasing.

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The maxim endures because it captures Edison’s entire working method in a single line. He built the first industrial research laboratory on the premise that invention was systematic grind, not lightning-strike genius — and he returned to the “inspiration and perspiration” formula repeatedly across a public career spanning the phonograph, the light bulb, and hundreds of other patents.

That it comes from Edison’s own mouth, in his own letters and interviews, is what sets it apart from the thousands of feel-good lines falsely pinned to famous names. The only honest caveat is the arithmetic: the ratio drifted from 2 %/98 % to the crisper 1 %/99 % that everyone now quotes.
